chapter_theme: Punishment belongs to rule, but dread does not. Disproportion, inaccessibility, a harsh face and harsh words turn subjects' fear into the slow or sudden ruin of the one who causes it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: what not causing dread means (561-562), the acts subjects fear and what they cost the king (563-567), what his own ministers fear (568), what the king himself comes to fear (569), and the overall fault (570).

561.reading: A king is one who weighs a case fairly and then punishes in proportion, so that the wrong does not go further.
561.nuance: The chapter opens by defining the king through punishment, not against it. As I read it, dread is set apart from penalty by inquiry and proportion; the two matching words தக்காங்கு and ஒத்தாங்கு carry the whole standard.

562.reading: Those who want their prosperity to last long should raise the rod sharply and bring it down lightly.
562.nuance: The rod image gives two audiences to one act: the raising is seen by would-be wrongdoers and the light landing by everyone else. If Manakkudavar is right, this verse softens the exact proportion that 561 has just asked for.

positions.position: Begin as if going beyond measure, then act within measure: the penalty remains proportionate and only looks mild beside its start.
positions.quote: அளவிறப்பச் செய்வார்போல் தொடங்கி; மெல்ல எறிக-செய்யுங்கால் அளவிறவாமல் செய்க

positions.position: The penalty should actually be less than the offence deserves.
positions.quote: இது குற்றத்திற்குத் தக்க தண்டத்தைக் குறையச் செய்யவேண்டு மென்றது.

positions.position: The severity lies in admonishing to prevent wrongs, and the gentleness in the punishing itself.
positions.quote: கண்டிக்கும்போது கடுமை காட்டித், தண்டிக்கும் போது மென்மை காட்டுகிறவர்களின்

563.reading: A cruel-sceptred ruler who goes on doing what terrifies people will certainly and quickly perish.
563.nuance: The verse supplies no mechanism: it asserts certainty (ஒருவந்தம்) and speed (ஒல்லை) and leaves the how to the verses that follow.

564.reading: A king about whom the painful words 'our lord is harsh' are spoken will quickly perish, his tenure cut short.
564.nuance: The harmful speech here is arguably the subjects', not the king's. A phrase people say of him can do what no enemy has done.

positions.position: The painful word is what wounded subjects say of the king, and உறை means his days: his life shrinks and his wealth goes.
உறை is where he dwells, which turns against him; even if land and residence bear it, divine force ruins him.
positions.quote: இது நாடும் தான் உறையும் இடமும் பொறுப்பினும் தெய்வத்தினாற் கெடுவ னென்றது.

positions.position: The harsh speech is the ruler's own, and what is lost is the regime's standing.
positions.quote: கடுஞ்சொல் உரைக்கும் கொடுங்கோல் என்று குடி மக்களால் கருதப்படும் அரசு

565.reading: The great wealth of one who is hard to get an audience with and grim of face has something of the ghost about it.
565.nuance: Inaccessibility and a grim face count as violence here, though no one has been touched.

positions.position: The wealth is as if a ghost had seized it: since no one approaches, it benefits neither him nor others.
The wealth is frightening, like seeing a ghost: no one will take from it, so no army gathers.
positions.quote: இது செல்வத்தை வாங்குவார் இன்மையின் படை சேராதென்றது.

566.reading: If a ruler is harsh of speech and without kindly regard, even vast wealth is lost on the spot instead of lasting.
566.nuance: நெடுஞ்செல்வம் and ஆங்கே are set against each other: length of holdings gives no length of time. This verse's instant loss sits oddly beside the slow filing of 567, so the chapter seems to offer no single speed of ruin.

567.reading: Harsh words and punishment past all bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength.
567.nuance: A file works by small repeated strokes, and here the king holds it against his own iron. Parimelazhagar assigns the harm: harsh words lose the army, and excessive punishment loses the country.

568.reading: The fortune of a king shrinks if he does not think matters through with his circle and then lashes out in anger.

positions.position: He leaves deliberation to his ministers without sharing it, then rages at them when it fails, and they withdraw from him in fear.
positions.quote: அமைச்சர்மேல் வைத்து அவரோடு தானும் எண்ணிச் செய்யாத அரசன்

positions.position: The context is justice: he does not examine others' offences together with his council, and acts from anger.
positions.quote: பிறர் செய்த குற்றத்தைத் தனக்கு இனமானாரோடே அமைந்து ஆராயாத அரசன்

positions.position: The fault is a failure to consult, followed by anger and crooked conduct, and the regime falls by itself.

569.reading: A king who has not made his defences will, when war comes, be seized by fear and quickly perish.
569.nuance: வெரு returns here pointed the other way: in a chapter on causing dread, the king himself ends up dreading. Manakkudavar draws this out by saying that a king must also not do what brings fear on himself.

570.reading: The harsh sceptre binds the unlearned to itself, and the earth carries no burden heavier than this.
570.nuance: Cruelty is presented as having a staffing logic: it gathers those who lack the learning to resist it. Parimelazhagar puts the weight on the alliance and Manakkudavar on the king who forms it, which comes to much the same.

links.note: 549 clears the king: punishing crime is no blemish but his work. 567 marks where that clearance ends, since punishment past the limit becomes a file on his own strength.
386 promises praise to the king who is easy to see and not harsh of speech. 565 and 566 cost out the opposite, turning two virtues into two ways of losing wealth.
382 lists fearlessness as a king's nature. 569 suggests that it also has a material condition: without prepared defences, even a king comes to fear.
The earth in 151 patiently bears even those who dig it, the model of forbearance. In 570 that same earth finds one burden too heavy, which gives the hyperbole its force.

source_issues: 563: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss reads செங்கோலன் where the verse has வெங்கோலன்; his own explanation then discusses வெங்கோலன், so this looks like a text error.
